title: Good News: AI Will Eat Application Software
author: Alex Immerman · Santiago Rodriguez

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts that AI’s value depends on embedding model capability in specific workflows rather than treating raw model intelligence or cheap code as sufficient. It materially extends the cluster by arguing that accumulated workflow knowledge and orchestration can become durable application-layer advantages, using Harvey as the legal-sector example. It does not, however, address verification or the jagged capability frontier directly.
qs: If Harvey deeply understands how a particular law firm structures its work—the templates, the review processes, the institutional preferences, the way a specific partner likes her memos done—there is simply no way a new entrant can replicate that overnight, even with the cost of code being zero.
So as the underlying models improve, Harvey’s orchestration layer—the scaffolding that routes model output through specific professional workflows—compound in value.

kp.k: Software market panic contrasts with authors' expansion thesis
kp.d: The authors report that public-software ETFs fell by 30 percent since the start of 2026 and that Salesforce, Adobe, Intuit, ServiceNow and Veeva fell 25 to 30 percent in weeks. They reject the reported market view that AI will kill software, predicting instead a larger industry with durable competitive advantages. This is an investment argument about the future, rather than a demonstrated industry outcome.
qs: Since the start of 2026, ETFs for public software companies have fallen by 30 percent, erasing all the gains since the launch of ChatGPT.
AI might increase competition; but it’ll also dramatically expand what software companies can do, how fast they can do it, and how large the markets they serve can become.
Software will be a much bigger industry, with durable competitive advantages for the companies that earn them.

kp.k: Cheaper code does not eliminate application business value
kp.d: The authors argue that software companies' value has never resided primarily in code, citing their survival against open-source software and cheap engineering labor. They report, rather than endorse, four bearish mechanisms: foundation-model labs taking over applications, enterprises building replacements internally, incumbents expanding into adjacent products, and new entrants undercutting prices. Agent purchasing focused on cheap task completion is another reported concern.
qs: The market is treating “software” as though it were a commodity input—as if the value of a software company resided in its code, and cheaper code meant more competition and therefore cheaper companies.
They would have been killed years ago by open-source software or by competition from cheap software engineering labor in developing countries.
The bearish arguments today usually fall into one of four categories.

kp.k: AI reduces switching barriers without necessarily shrinking profits
kp.d: Using Hamilton Helmer's Seven Powers framework, the authors identify switching costs as a competitive advantage particularly exposed to AI. Agents can assist migration, putting pressure on vendors dependent on lock-in. They predict customer redistribution, better products and faster innovation, while asserting that aggregate industry profit pools need not suffer.
qs: It’s definitely true that AI is changing the friction and the cost-benefit analysis associated with switching vendors: agents can assist with a lot of migration work that used to be a headache.
We expect AI will shift some customers to new winners, but it won’t impair industry profit pools at large: companies will just *get better*.

kp.k: Legal collaboration platforms may gain stronger network effects
kp.d: The authors describe Salesforce and Figma as examples of ecosystem and collaboration advantages, and identify Harvey and Hebbia as developing finance and legal collaboration spaces connecting providers and clients. They anticipate agents joining those spaces and argue that greater participation increases platform value. The claim that AI will strengthen these effects is a prediction, not a quantified finding.
qs: Harvey and Hebbia are building finance and legal collaboration spaces that connect service providers and clients, and soon their agents, on a single system: the more people and agents who use these platforms, the more valuable the platforms become.
As migration gets easier, aggregation gets easier, but these network effects simply don’t go away in a world where software is free.

kp.k: Compute costs and shared infrastructure can reinforce scale
kp.d: The authors suggest scale may matter more for AI applications when compute spending exceeds labor costs, giving large token consumers unit-cost advantages. They also argue that centralized maintenance and specialization remain valuable, illustrating shared compliance and payment optimization with Stripe. Hardware-linked companies such as Anduril, Flock Safety and Waymo are cited as additional beneficiaries of volume-based cost reductions.
qs: But to some extent, it may matter more for AI applications where compute spend exceeds labor costs, driving a unit cost advantage to the larger consumers of tokens.

Its compliance infrastructure absorbs the cost of navigating regulations across dozens of countries so that individual businesses don’t have to; its payment optimization algorithms, which route and retry transactions to maximize authorization rates, improve with every dollar of volume—and they can pass those savings on to their customers.

kp.k: Human accountability may preserve brands despite agent purchasing
kp.d: The authors predict that proliferation of AI-built products could increase the value of trusted brands, particularly in business-critical functions. They qualify this argument by acknowledging that price-optimizing purchasing agents may change brand effects, but maintain that agents reporting to accountable humans will not eliminate enterprise preferences for trusted suppliers.
qs: Brand is how you signal reliability in a world of infinite optionality.
We do acknowledge the power of brand might *change* as more decisions are delegated to AI agents that optimize for price without the soft considerations that humans have (agent-led growth!).
But as long as they report to humans who have to worry about getting fired, the “no one got fired for buying IBM” principle still holds.

kp.k: Proprietary legal data remains a potential competitive advantage
kp.d: The authors distinguish easily replicated public-data interfaces from scarce, high-quality proprietary data. They argue that AI increases the latter's value by enabling more uses, citing VLex's legal database alongside Bloomberg, Abridge and OpenEvidence. These are illustrative observations without quantitative evidence of the competitive effects.
qs: If friction goes to zero, simply consolidating publicly available data into a usable interface becomes less valuable, because anyone can do it.
But if AI enables doing *much more* with high-quality data than you could before, then the stuff that you can’t get easily becomes *extremely* valuable.
We have observed the power of Bloomberg’s live market data, Abridge’s millions of clinical conversations, OpenEvidence’s vast medical library, and VLex’s legal database.

kp.k: Embedded legal workflows can strengthen Harvey's application layer
kp.d: The authors present process power, termed process engineering by Hebbia's George Sivulka, as potentially the strongest AI-era advantage. Their conditional Harvey example concerns understanding a law firm's templates, review processes, institutional preferences and individual partner expectations. They argue that this knowledge becomes more valuable as applications execute work rather than merely record it, and that better models enhance the orchestration layer rather than render it redundant.
qs: Successful app software companies are the ones that co-evolve with their clients around these workflows.

If Harvey deeply understands how a particular law firm structures its work—the templates, the review processes, the institutional preferences, the way a specific partner likes her memos done—there is simply no way a new entrant can replicate that overnight, even with the cost of code being zero.
That kind of embedded workflow knowledge becomes *more* powerful, not less, as software moves from a system of record to a system of action, because you can just do much more with that knowledge.
Better models don’t make the application layer thinner: they make it *more capable*, because the hard part was never raw intelligence. It was knowing what to do with it.

kp.k: Agent pricing can counterposition entrants against seat-based incumbents
kp.d: The authors argue that task-replacing agents create opportunities for entrants whose business models incumbents cannot easily adopt without cannibalizing revenue. In customer service, they report that Decagon charges per conversation and predict eventual per-resolution pricing, contrasting this with Zendesk's seat-based revenue. They view this as better incentive alignment and invoke Netflix versus Blockbuster and Workday versus Peoplesoft as analogies, without claiming that aggregate pricing power must decline.
qs: The “agent” model of doing work and replacing tasks is certainly going to create some counterposition opportunities for new startups to challenge incumbents.

Decagon prices its customer support product per conversation handled, not per agent seat, and will eventually price per resolution achieved: that’s fundamentally a better alignment of incentives between vendor and buyer.
An incumbent like Zendesk can’t easily make that same move without cannibalizing its own seat-based revenue.

kp.k: Margin uncertainty accompanies predicted expansion into underserved workflows
kp.d: The authors leave future margins unresolved: easier switching could weaken vendor pricing power, while more efficient labor use could expand margins. They nevertheless predict substantial market growth as cheaper code enables adjacent offerings, more complex automation and economically viable service to previously low-ACV customers. This concerns software-market expansion, not a demonstrated improvement in access to legal assistance.
qs: Maybe gross margins settle into a different steady-state: maybe pricing power is diminished because switching costs give procurement teams more leverage in vendor negotiations, but AI also supports margin expansion due to a much more efficient use of labor.
Companies will be able to serve more customers, enter adjacent markets, and automate workflows that were previously far too complex or too expensive to touch.
Customers that were previously too low ACV will suddenly have attractive economics.

kp.k: AI bifurcates software markets rather than protecting every incumbent
kp.d: The authors explicitly predict losses for thin interfaces around commodity functions, archaic systems of record that continually raise prices, and vendors with inferior pricing models or value propositions. Their optimism is conditional on delivering substantive customer value rather than relying on lock-in: some companies will adapt, others will fail, while the wider ecosystem grows.
qs: Frontend tools that serve primarily as thin wrappers around commodity functionality and do relatively little beyond presenting data in a slightly more convenient format are vulnerable.
Incumbent systems of record that still operate on archaic interfaces but raise prices every year should be worried.
The companies that win in this environment will be the ones delivering genuine value, not the ones that built the highest walls around their customer base.
So yes, some individual companies will lose. But the industry will win, and win big.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Immerman and Rodriguez predict that AI will substantially expand application software rather than destroy the industry's business model or aggregate profit pools.
pts.d: The authors argue that software companies derive value from more than code, so cheaper code does not necessarily eliminate pricing power or durable businesses. They expect AI to increase competition while expanding product capabilities, development speed and addressable markets. They predict that providers will serve customers previously uneconomic because of low annual contract values, enter adjacent markets and automate previously prohibitively complex or expensive workflows. These are application-software claims, not predictions about law-firm revenues or legal employment.

pts.k: The authors predict easier vendor switching and a split between vulnerable software businesses and providers delivering defensible value.
pts.d: AI agents are said to reduce migration work, weakening vendor lock-in and pressuring legacy providers dependent on captive customers. The authors expect customer redistribution rather than an industry-wide reduction in profit pools, with competition producing better products and faster innovation. They identify thin interfaces over commodity functionality, archaic systems of record that repeatedly increase prices, and inferior legacy pricing models as vulnerable. Some incumbents will adapt; others will fail. They leave the eventual margin outcome uncertain because reduced pricing power could coexist with labor-efficiency gains.

pts.k: The authors claim that collaboration and ecosystem network effects persist under AI and may strengthen, including on legal and finance platforms.
pts.d: They describe Harvey and Hebbia as building collaboration spaces connecting service providers and clients, with agents expected to join soon. They argue that additional participants make these platforms more valuable and that AI can increase what participants accomplish through a network. Salesforce and Figma illustrate existing ecosystem and collaboration effects; EliseAI illustrates a multi-sided network. Harvey and Hebbia are discussed as software platforms, not as alternative legal service providers.

pts.k: The authors predict that proprietary data and embedded professional-workflow knowledge become more valuable as AI improves, using VLex and Harvey as legal-sector examples.
pts.d: They distinguish easily reproduced aggregation of public data from difficult-to-obtain, high-quality proprietary resources, citing VLex's legal database among the latter examples. Their Harvey argument is explicitly conditional: if its platform deeply understands a firm's templates, review processes, institutional preferences and partner-specific requirements, a competitor cannot immediately reproduce that knowledge even with free code. As software executes work rather than merely recording it, they predict that this knowledge and the orchestration of model outputs through professional workflows will compound in value. The source does not establish that Harvey already possesses this depth of knowledge at every client firm.

pts.k: The authors argue that AI can strengthen scale advantages and trusted brands, while qualifying both predictions.
pts.d: Scale may become more important where AI applications spend more on compute than labor, giving large token purchasers lower unit costs. Centralized maintenance, specialized infrastructure and hardware production are also presented as continuing sources of scale advantages. An influx of inexpensive, rapidly built competing products may increase the value of brands that signal reliability, especially for business-critical functions. The authors acknowledge that purchasing agents focused on price may alter brand effects, but expect human accountability for procurement decisions to preserve their importance.

pts.k: The authors predict that task-performing agents create opportunities for startups with usage- or outcome-based pricing to challenge seat-based incumbents.
pts.d: They argue that incumbents may find competing business models unattractive because adopting them would cannibalize existing revenues. In customer support, they describe Decagon's current per-conversation pricing and predict eventual pricing per resolution achieved, contrasting this with Zendesk's seat-based economics. They regard such pricing as better aligning buyer and vendor incentives, while arguing that shifts between business models need not reduce eventual market-wide pricing power. This is a software-vendor pricing claim, not a claim about legal billable hours or law-firm alternative fee arrangements.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source supports its predictions chiefly with a competitive-advantage framework, company illustrations, author observations and historical analogies, rather than quantified tests of AI's business effects.
pts.d: Immerman and Rodriguez organize their argument around Hamilton Helmer's Seven Powers and discuss counterpositioning using disruption theory and historical comparisons such as Netflix versus Blockbuster and Workday versus PeopleSoft. Salesforce, Figma, Stripe, Harvey, Hebbia, VLex and Decagon supply illustrative business cases. The authors explicitly invoke their observations about proprietary-data businesses, but provide no underlying measurements for the claimed network, workflow or data advantages. The opening reports a 30 percent fall in public-software ETFs since the start of 2026 and 25–30 percent falls in selected companies; these establish the market-panic context, not realized evidence for the predicted expansion. No legal-task benchmarks, measured legal productivity gains, law-firm adoption study or quantified forecast of future software profits is presented. The article is an argument by a16z Growth investors, with the claims attributed to its two authors rather than to people they quote.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The March 2, 2026 article mixes present-tense descriptions with open-ended transition forecasts; it supplies no dated endpoint for market expansion.
pts.d: Current descriptions include AI-assisted migration, emerging collaboration platforms and Decagon's per-conversation pricing. Agents joining collaboration spaces are expected 'soon'; resolution-based pricing is expected 'eventually.' Industry expansion is placed after the AI transition or current panic without a specified year. The Harvey prediction depends on deep firm-specific workflow understanding and improving underlying models. Stronger network effects depend on AI making networks more useful; scale advantages are conditional on compute economics; brand durability is qualified by human oversight of purchasing agents. The authors acknowledge individual business failures, possible pricing pressure and uncertain steady-state margins despite their confident aggregate growth forecast.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The main affected groups are application-software vendors, AI-native entrants and enterprise buyers; legal-sector implications concern platforms, participating firms and their clients.
pts.d: Legacy vendors relying on lock-in, thin functionality or seat-based economics face competitive pressure. AI-native entrants gain opportunities through differentiated workflows and business models, while trusted, data-rich, networked or operationally embedded providers may become more defensible. Enterprise customers and procurement teams gain easier switching, more pricing-model choice and potentially better products; previously uneconomic customer segments become attractive to serve. For legal services specifically, law firms, individual partners, service providers and clients appear as participants whose workflows, preferences and collaboration increase platform value for Harvey and related systems. VLex appears as a legal-data resource. The source does not predict changes in lawyer headcount, junior training, firm staffing structures, human verification duties, access to justice or legal-service fees.
